growth_story.headline: Iceland's bank boom ended in the 2008 crash; tourism and workers from abroad then lifted output, but income per person has grown slowly since.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 1997 income per person grew 0.5 percent a year, with falls in 1991 and 1992 that the sources gathered here do not explain. From 1998 to 2007 growth ran at 3.7 percent a year while the newly private banks grew far larger than the economy, and credit to the private sector rose from 61.4 percent of GDP in 1998 to 301.0 percent in 2006. The three big banks collapsed in 2008, income per person fell 8.6 percent in 2009, and it did not get back to its 2007 level until 2016. Recovery after that rested on a tourism boom and on workers arriving from abroad, so total output grew faster than income per person, and growth from 2008 to 2025 averaged only 0.4 percent a year, including a fall of 8.1 percent in the pandemic year 2020. Income per person bounced back to a peak in 2023, then fell in 2024 and 2025 amid high inflation, tight policy and one-off shocks, and in 2025 it was 1.7 percent below that peak.

threads.title: Bank boom and crash
threads.text: After the banks were privatized, their assets grew to many times the size of the economy, and credit to the private sector reached 301.0 percent of GDP in 2006. Within a week in 2008 the three main banks failed; income per person fell 8.6 percent in 2009 and fell again in 2010, and years of repairing balance sheets followed.

growth_story.tension: The IMF describes a decade of output growth among the highest in advanced economies, driven by tourism and construction, but in the data income per person grew only 1.0 percent a year over 2016 to 2025, last among its 11 structural peers. The gap is the population: output grew mostly through more workers, many from abroad, rather than through more output per person, and the IMF itself says gains in living standards have been more modest than output growth.
